platelet phosphatidylcholines are hydrolyzed by phospholipase D, which generates phosphatidate and phosphatidylserine, and that the hydrolysis by this enzyme is stimulated by thrombin and by Ca2+.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of cytoplasm free Ca2+ concentration on the activity of phospholipase enzymes in human platelets.
the role of Ca2+ in the regulation of platelet phospholipes A2 and C activities.
the effects of quinquinolinic acid (QQA) on the activity of the enzymes of glycolysis, citric acid cycle and pentose phosphate shunt in rat brain homogenates.

the Ca2+ concentrations necessary to elicit a maximal activity of phospholipase(s) A2 and C in stimulated human platelets are in the range of 1-5 and 0.2-1 microM, respectively.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the cytosolic calcium concentration required to activate phospholipase-A2 is higher than the concentration required for activation of phospholipase-C, and that the cytoplasmic concentration of Ca2+ in thrombin-stimulated platelets is sufficient to activate phospholipes A2 but not phospholipase c.
the cytoplasmic Ca2+ concentration required to fully activate human platelet phosphatidylcholinespecific phospholipase is in the micromolar range.
phospholipase activation in platelets is a Ca2+-dependent process, but that phospholipases C and A2 have different Ca2+ requirements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the calcium concentration required for phospholipase activation is different for different phospholipases.
phospholipase activity in platelets is regulated by calcium.

phospholipases are not all equally sensitive to Ca2+ and that the Ca2+ concentration required for the activation of phospholipase(s) may be higher than that required to activate other Ca2+-requiring enzymes.
